title: How the yam was tamed, and the four days
description: Why the Igbo count in fours: the yam was domesticated and still no one knew when to plant it, until the four strangers came with the count — Eke, Oye, Afọ, Nkwo.
html:
HOW THE YAM WAS TAMED, AND HOW THE FOUR DAYS WERE LEARNED (Aikọ ke Ji na ke Ubọchị Anọ)

I.

In the beginning the yam was not a farm thing. It grew in the bush by itself, twining up the trees where no hand put it, and the people ate it when they found it. A man would walk a whole day and come home with two tubers. A woman would dig where last year's rain had softened the ground, and find nothing. The yam was wild and it was free, and it fed no one who did not spend the day hunting it.

Then Ndi Igbo began to look at the yam the way a man looks at a woman he means to marry. They watched where it came up. They saw that it liked the loose earth at the edge of the bush, that it climbed, that the little ones grew at the head of the big one. They took the small tubers and put them back into the ground nearer the compound. They cleared the bush around them and heaped the soil at their feet. They cut sticks and set them for the vines to climb, and the vine climbed and the tuber swelled under the soil.

So the yam was tamed. But a tamed thing is a thing you must keep, and keeping it began the trouble, because nobody knew WHEN. The vine gave no warning. A man could plant and the rain would come too early and rot the set in the ground. Another could wait, and the rain would come and go while the soil still held his yam in its hand, and the harvest would be small and bitter. Some years the whole farm was a loss, and a family that had tamed the yam found itself poorer than the family that still went to the bush for it.

They tried everything a man tries. They watched the moon and it lied to them. They watched the iroko and the new leaf, and the leaf came early one year and late another. A diviner would throw on one side and a diviner on the other, and both would be right and both wrong. There was one year of hunger in every four, and the hunger was always the same hunger: not of land, not of seed, not of rain, but of COUNTING. The people had the yam and did not have the days.

II.

It was in that time that four strangers came. They did not come to the palace, or they came to the compound of a man and not to a king, and this is how the old people tell it: they came carrying gifts, and they would not say their names.

Some say the host grew tired of asking, and set a rat in each one's basket in the night, and by morning each man's basket told his name. Others say the names were given freely in the morning, as a blessing, when the guests saw the hunger in the house. Both are told. What is not disputed is the four names:

Eke · Oye · Afọ · Nkwo

They said: you have tamed the yam, and you do not know when to plant it. So count. Let these four be your count, and let the fourth be a rest and a market, and begin the count again. Number your days in fours, and number your planting in the same fours, and you will know when the season turns because the season will be a number in your hand and not a guess in your belly.

And they showed it: four days to the market, and four fours to the turning of the planting. The day you set the yam, count the fours; when the count reaches the number that was shown, the yam is ready to be lifted, and no sooner. The planting was no longer a feeling. It was a count, and a count can be taught to a child.

Then they went. Nobody saw which road.

III.

So the four days are not only a market week. They are the answer to the hunger. Eke is the day the count begins, Oye the second, Afọ the third, Nkwo the fourth and the rest, and when Nkwo is finished the count starts again at Eke — and the yam, whose season was a mystery, is held inside the same four as everything else a household does.

This is why the four days are shared by every Igbo town and why no one town may change them. A man may leave his father's town and go where his mother was born, and the count will be the same count, and he will know when to plant. The four days belong to no king. They belong to the yam, and to the hunger that was answered.

Eke · Oye · Afọ · Nkwo

Four days. One count. Every town. And the yam, at last, in the hand of the count.
